title: The Speed Camera That Never Measures Your Speed
central_question: If an average speed camera never measures your speed, how does it know you were speeding, and why doesn't braking at the camera help?
fiction_notice: Illustration. The plate, times and journey are invented examples.

scenes.narration: Everyone brakes for the speed camera. But this one never measures your speed. It checks a clock. Twice.
scenes.caption: This camera never measures your speed.

scenes.narration: Two miles back, you passed this. It fires an infrared flash you can't see. Your number plate bounces it straight back. Plate read. Time stamped.
scenes.caption: Invisible infrared. Plate read. Time stamped.

scenes.narration: Now the clock runs. Two miles away, a second camera is waiting. At fifty, that takes at least two minutes twenty-four.
scenes.caption: 2 miles at 50 mph takes at least 2:24.

scenes.narration: Camera two reads your plate again. Two miles in two minutes flat. That's an average of sixty.
scenes.caption: 2 miles in 2:00 = average 60 mph.

scenes.narration: "So I'll just brake at the camera." Watch. Seventy most of the way. Forty for the camera. Same two minutes. Still sixty. The camera never saw your brakes.
scenes.caption: Braking at the end can't undo the clock.

scenes.narration: Every car gets the same treatment. Legal? Your record is deleted. Too fast? Both photos become evidence.
scenes.caption: Legal: deleted. Too fast: both photos become evidence.

scenes.narration: But a different police camera network keeps its reads. Around twenty-five million a day. Stored for up to a year.
scenes.caption: Police ANPR: ~25 million reads a day, kept up to a year.

scenes.narration: So where was your car last Tuesday?
scenes.caption: So where was your car last Tuesday?

claims.text: Average speed (point-to-point) cameras do not measure instantaneous speed. Cameras at two or more points read each vehicle's number plate (ANPR) with a time stamp; the system divides the known distance by the time taken.
ANPR cameras use infrared illumination and imaging, which lets them read plates day and night; at least one widely used system takes an infrared image at the entry camera.
UK number plates are retroreflective, returning light (including infrared) towards its source, which ANPR relies on.

Worked example: 2.0 miles at a 50 mph limit takes at least 144 s (2:24). Covering it in 120 s is an average of 60 mph. 70 mph for 14/9 mile (about 1.56 mi) plus 40 mph for 4/9 mile (about 0.44 mi) also takes exactly 120 s, so braking for the last section still averages 60 mph.

For vehicles that do not exceed the average speed limit, the plate data and images are automatically deleted; for speeding vehicles an evidence record with ANPR data, images and time stamps from both cameras is produced.
Police ANPR cameras in the UK submit roughly 25 to 35 million read records a day to the national system (NPCC / Surveillance Camera Commissioner figures; capacity is higher).
Read records on the National ANPR Service are deleted 12 months after entry unless preserved for an investigation.
